advisor.summary: Reg. §1.469-1T(e)(3)(ii)(A) takes a property out of the §469 'rental activity' definition when the average period of customer use is seven days or less: the per-se passive label never attaches, and real estate professional status is unnecessary. From there the activity is tested like any other business — material participation under Reg. §1.469-5T(a) renders the losses non-passive against W-2 and business income, which is what lets a high earner pair a short-term rental with cost segregation and 100% bonus depreciation for a large first-year offset. The limits are equally mechanical. Substantial hotel-like services push the activity onto Schedule C and into self-employment tax under Reg. §1.1402(a)-4, personal use beyond the §280A thresholds imposes its own cap, and the average-stay computation must be re-run every year. Pohoski marks both edges — material participation carried some properties and failed others on the hour evidence. The engine models qualification by moving the rental's result out of the passive bucket.
mechanics: Divide total guest-occupied days by the number of stays: an average of seven days or less takes the property outside the rental definition under Reg. §1.469-1T(e)(3)(ii)(A), while a thirty-day average paired with significant personal services is a second, narrower entry point.

Once outside the rental definition, ordinary material participation controls under Reg. §1.469-5T(a): 500 hours, substantially-all participation, or more than 100 hours and more than any other individual — with cleaners, co-hosts, and managers counted on the other side of the ledger.
Self-management is the practical requirement: a full-service management company typically out-participates the owner and defeats the more-than-anyone-else test.
Pairing supplies the power: 5/7/15-year components reclassified by a cost segregation study take 100% bonus under §168(k), generating a first-year non-passive loss against high W-2 income.

Absent substantial services — daily cleaning during stays, meals, concierge — the activity remains on Schedule E and outside self-employment tax under Reg. §1.1402(a)-4; hotel-like services shift it to Schedule C and into the SE tax base.
Personal use above the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days triggers the §280A vacation-home limits — a second cap that operates independently of §469.

authority.note: Average customer use of seven days or less removes the activity from the per-se rental definition — the entry point.
The material participation tests; short-term-rental owners most often rely on 500 hours, substantially-all, or more-than-100-and-most.
The passive-loss regime and the per-se rental rule the exception avoids.
100% bonus depreciation on reclassified short-life components — the source of the first-year loss.
Excludes rental real estate from self-employment income unless substantial services are rendered to occupants — the Schedule C tripwire.
The vacation-home rules: excess personal use caps deductions however the passive-loss question resolves.
Short-term condo rentals tested for material participation — the taxpayers won where the hour evidence held and lost where it did not.

requirements: Average guest stay of seven days or less, computed from booking records and documented.
Material participation by the owner or spouse under an identified §1.469-5T(a) test, supported by contemporaneous hour logs for the owner and every service provider.
Operations substantially self-managed: the owner handles guest communication, pricing, and turnover arrangements.
Personal use held within the §280A limits so no second loss cap applies.
risks: Hour substantiation is the leading audit theory: under the more-than-100-hours-and-more-than-anyone-else test the IRS weighs cleaners’ and co-hosts’ hours against the owner’s, and Pohoski v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 1998-17, split property by property on precisely that evidence — contemporaneous logs for the owner and every vendor are the defense.
Substantial services convert the activity to Schedule C and self-employment tax, eroding the benefit — the service menu is a tax decision, not merely hospitality.
The average-stay test resets annually: a single winter of month-long tenants can push the property back to per-se passive.
Acceleration is borrowed, not free — later-year depreciation shrinks, and recapture follows at sale.
Local ordinances, permits, and lodging taxes form a parallel compliance layer the income tax analysis never reaches.
stateNotes: Conformity: states inherit the federal passive-loss result through their federal starting points, but some states decouple from bonus depreciation and slow the paired deduction at the state level — screen both rules together.
Missouri conforms on both fronts through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121); separately, Missouri short-term rentals owe state and local lodging taxes as an operational matter.
PTET interaction: none in the standard structure — a directly held short-term rental falls outside every PTET regime; the analysis changes only when the activity runs through an electing entity.
reviewChecklist: Average stay computed from the year's actual booking data and documented.
Material participation test identified; owner and vendor hour logs sampled for quality.
Service menu measured against the substantial-services line; Schedule E position confirmed.
Personal-use days reconciled to the §280A limits.
Paired cost segregation and bonus amounts sized to the loss the client can actually absorb.

client.teaser: Short-term rentals follow their own tax rules — their losses can offset your paycheck.
client.headline: A short-term rental can shelter your W-2 income
plainEnglish: Rental losses normally cannot touch your salary. The main exception is for people whose career is real estate — which leaves out most people with full-time jobs.

Short-term rentals work differently. If guests stay an average of seven days or less — the normal vacation-rental pattern — the tax law does not treat the property as a rental at all. It counts as a business. Run it yourself, and its losses can offset your regular income.

Add a study that front-loads the property’s depreciation, and a new short-term rental can produce a large first-year deduction against a large salary. You do have to run the place yourself — bookings, guests, turnovers — and log your hours as you go.
client.analogy: Think of it as a side door into the same room the full-time real estate pros use. It opens when guests stay about a week or less and you run the show yourself.
benefits: Losses can offset your salary and business income — no career change required
Pairs with accelerated depreciation for a large first-year write-off
The property stays a real, income-producing investment
steps: WE confirm your booking pattern qualifies — an average stay of seven days or less.
WE coordinate the depreciation study and claim the first-year deduction.
WE monitor the details that could change the result — services, personal use, stay lengths.
YOU run the property hands-on and log your hours as you go.
clientCommitments: Manage the property yourself, at least in the loss year
Log your hours and keep vendor invoices that show their hours
Stay within the personal-use limits we set
Keep guest services simple — talk to us before adding hotel-style daily service

annualMaintenance: Annual average-stay computation from the year's booking data
Hour-log review before filing the return
Personal-use and service-level check against the claimed treatment
deliverables: Qualification memo covering average stay, participation test, and service level
Hour-tracking template for the owner and vendors
Depreciation schedule coordinated with the cost segregation study
